01.note: A man insisted, twice, that he would show another man's straw to the gentile authorities, though Rav forbade it; Rav Kahana, sitting before Rav, broke his neck and killed him. Warning that the new Greek rulers punish bloodshed, Rav sent Kahana to the Land of Israel to study under Rabbi Yoḥanan, on condition he raise no objections for seven years. Kept silent, Kahana was moved back to the last row, then stood up and out-argued Rabbi Yoḥanan, who removed his seven cushions one by one. Seeing Kahana's split lips, Rabbi Yoḥanan thought he was smirking; he was offended and Kahana died. Told it was only his look, Rabbi Yoḥanan got past a serpent at the burial cave by calling himself the disciple, prayed, and raised Kahana, who answered all his questions.
01.why: The Gemara is discussing who must pay when someone hands another's property to gentile officials; this story shows how gravely the Sages treated a man who would inform on a fellow Jew's property, and a run of informer cases follows.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher who forbade the man to inform, then sent Rav Kahana away to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's student, who killed the would-be informer and later out-argued Rabbi Yoḥanan.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Also called Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish; he reviewed Rabbi Yoḥanan's lecture and called Rav Kahana a lion.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Head of the academy in the Land of Israel; an old man whose offense caused Rav Kahana's death, and who revived him.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.
A legal ruling or teaching of Jewish law.
Rabbi Yoḥanan sat raised on cushions so all the students could see him; removing them one by one lowered himself before Rav Kahana.

02.note: Someone showed Rabbi Abba's silk to gentiles, who seized it. Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa sat to judge whether the informer must pay, with Rabbi Ile'a beside them. They thought to hold him liable, from a mishna that a judge who rules wrongly pays from his own pocket, but Rabbi Ile'a quoted Rav that this applies only when the judge took and handed over the money himself. They sent Rabbi Abba to Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim and Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat, who held the informer liable.
02.why: The Gemara is collecting cases of people who pointed out a fellow Jew's property to gentiles; this one asks whether causing a loss by words alone, without taking the property, brings an obligation to pay.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The owner of the silk that was seized.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: One of the three judges who first heard the case.

people.name: Rabbi Ile’a
people.about: Sat beside the judges and quoted Rav to limit the mishna they relied on.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim
people.about: One of two judges who rule on indirect damage, and who held the informer liable.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
people.about: The other judge who rules on indirect damage, and held the informer liable.

terms.meaning: The early collection of rabbinic law on which the Gemara is a commentary; also a single teaching from it.
Loss a person causes without doing the harm with his own hands; some judges held people liable for it and some did not.

03.note: A man was holding a purse of money collected to ransom captives. Thieves came upon him, and he took the purse and gave it to them. Rabba exempted him from paying it back. Abaye objected that the man had saved himself with someone else's money; Rabba answered that there is no greater redemption of captives than this.
03.why: It is one of a series of cases before Rabba about people who give up another's property to save themselves; just before, a man who handed thieves a deposited silver cup was judged by whether he was rich.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The judge who exempted the man.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objected that the man saved himself with another's property.

terms.meaning: Paying ransom to free Jews held captive, counted among the most important uses of charity money.

04.note: A man hurried his donkey onto a ferry before the other passengers boarded. The donkey was about to sink the boat, so another man pushed it into the river and it drowned. Rabba exempted him from paying. Abaye objected that he had saved himself with another's property; Rabba answered that the donkey's owner had been a pursuer from the start.
04.why: The Gemara notes this fits Rabba's general rule: a pursuer's property may be destroyed to save his victim, but a person may not save himself with a bystander's property.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The judge who exempted the man who drowned the donkey.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objected that the man saved himself with another's property.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, someone who puts another person's life in danger; he may be stopped by any means needed, including destroying his property.

05.note: Rav Ḥisda had a sharecropper who would weigh out the produce and give Rav Ḥisda his share, and weigh it and take his own. Rav Ḥisda dismissed him, and applied to him the verse "the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the righteous" (Proverbs 13:22).
05.why: It follows a dispute over whether an informer's property may be destroyed, where one view cites a verse that what the wicked prepare the just will wear; Rav Ḥisda cites a similar verse about a sinner's wealth passing to the righteous.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Owner of the field, who dismissed his sharecropper.

terms.meaning: A tenant who farms someone else's field in return for a share of the crop.

06.note: When Ravina came to Bei Meḥoza, the women of the town tossed chains and bracelets before him as charity, and he accepted them. Rabba Tosfa'a objected that charity collectors may accept only small gifts from women, not large ones. Ravina answered that for the people of Meḥoza, these were small things.
06.why: The discussion has just quoted the teaching that charity collectors may take only small gifts from women, since they may lack permission to give away costly things; this story tests how that rule applies.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who collected charity in Bei Meḥoza.

people.name: Rabba Tosfa’a
people.about: Challenged Ravina for accepting jewelry from women.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna.

07.note: People gave a shepherd their animals every day in front of witnesses. One day they handed them over without witnesses, and at day's end he denied ever receiving them. Then witnesses testified that he had eaten two of them. Rabbi Zeira said that by Rabbi Ḥiyya's first ruling, an oath is due about the rest. Abaye objected: is this shepherd, now shown to be a robber, to be trusted to swear? Rabbi Zeira answered that he meant the other side swears and collects.
07.why: The Sages are debating whether witnesses who prove part of a claim, like a defendant who admits part, oblige him to swear about the rest; Rabbi Zeira applies Rabbi Ḥiyya's view to this shepherd.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Applied Rabbi Ḥiyya's ruling to the shepherd's case.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objected that a proven robber cannot be trusted to take an oath.

terms.meaning: In a money dispute, a court can require a party to swear to his claim before God; swearing falsely is a grave sin, so an oath settles the matter.
Here, the owners of the animals: when the defendant cannot be trusted to swear, the claimant swears instead and collects.

08.note: Two people were arguing over a bathhouse, each saying it was his. One of them consecrated it to the Temple. Rav Ḥananya, Rav Oshaya and all the Rabbis stayed away from it, and Rav Oshaya asked Rabba to put the question to Rav Ḥisda in Kafrei. On the way, in Sura, Rav Hamnuna told Rabba the answer was in a mishna: an animal that may or may not be a firstborn stays with its owner, yet may not be sheared or worked. Whether that settles the bathhouse is argued out in what follows.
08.why: The Gemara is asking whether a person can consecrate a disputed item that he has not seized; this bathhouse case is brought as the answer.

people.name: Rav Oshaya
people.about: Kept away from the bathhouse and asked Rabba to take the question to Rav Ḥisda.

people.name: Rav Ḥananya
people.about: Also kept away from the consecrated bathhouse.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Carried the question; in Sura he heard Rav Hamnuna's answer.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage in Sura who pointed to a mishna about firstborn animals.

terms.meaning: To dedicate property to the Temple; after that, using it for oneself is forbidden.
A firstborn male animal of a kosher species is holy and goes to a priest; a firstborn son is redeemed from a priest.
The early collection of rabbinic law on which the Gemara comments; also a single teaching from it.

09.note: Rabban Gamliel and other Elders were traveling on a ship. Rabban Gamliel declared that a tenth of his produce, to be measured out later, was given to Yehoshua, and the place where it lay was rented to him; and another tenth was given to Akiva ben Yosef to acquire for the poor, its place also rented to him.
09.why: Ulla has said a person's field acquires things for him only when he stands next to it; Rabbi Abba cites this voyage to challenge him, since Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva were on the ship, far from the field.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Gave away his tithes while at sea.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Yehoshua ben Ḥananya, a Levite, who received the first tithe.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Akiva ben Yosef, who received the poor man's tithe on behalf of the poor.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Raised this incident as an objection to Ulla.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage whose ruling about acquiring through one's field is challenged.

terms.meaning: A tenth of the harvest that must be set aside: the first tithe goes to a Levite, and in certain years another tithe goes to the poor.
A member of the tribe of Levi, entitled to receive the first tithe.
Here, the leading Sages traveling with Rabban Gamliel.

10.note: A bill of divorce was found in Rav Huna's court, stating it was written in Sheviri City on the Rakhis River. Rav Huna said they must worry there might be two towns called Sheviri, so it could belong to someone else. Rav Ḥisda told Rabba to look into it, since Rav Huna would ask him that evening. Rabba went out, examined the question, and found a mishna: any court document that is found must be returned.
10.why: The Gemara argues that even where caravans pass often, a found bill of divorce is held back only if two people of the same name are known to live there; Rabba's ruling in Rav Huna's busy court is its proof.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Head of the court where the bill of divorce was found.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Told Rabba to research the question before Rav Huna asked him.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Found the mishna that settled the case.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end their marriage.
A document produced or confirmed by a court; the mishna says a found one must be returned.

11.note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana lost a bill of divorce he had been given to deliver, in the study hall. When it was found, he said he could give a distinguishing mark for it, and could also recognize it by sight, and it was returned to him. Afterward he said he did not know which had decided it: whether they hold that distinguishing marks count by Torah law, or whether they trusted his recognition only because he is a Torah scholar, which would not be done for an ordinary person.
11.why: Rav Ashi has just said a found bill of divorce is returned only on a clear-cut mark, since it is uncertain whether marks are trusted by Torah law; Rabba bar bar Ḥana's own case leaves that same question open.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: A Sage who lost a bill of divorce he was delivering and got it back.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end their marriage.
A specific feature an owner can describe to prove a found item is his.
Knowing an item by sight without being able to name a specific mark; the Sages trusted this only from Torah scholars.
A rule from the Torah itself, as opposed to one the Sages instituted, which is treated more leniently.

12.note: A bill of divorce found in Rav Huna's court said it was written in Sheviri City on the Rakhis River. Rav Huna worried there might be two towns called Sheviri. Rav Ḥisda sent Rabba to look into it before Rav Huna asked him that evening, and Rabba found the mishna that any court document must be returned. Rav Amram asked how Rabba could settle a ritual matter from a teaching about money. Rabba called him a fool: the mishna also covers documents of ḥalitza and refusal. Then the cedar beam of the study hall gave way, and each of the two said it was because of him.
12.why: The mishna says found court documents must be returned; this incident shows Rabba applying that line to a bill of divorce, and defending the step from money matters to ritual ones.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Head of the court where the bill of divorce was found.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sent Rabba to research the question.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Found the answer in the mishna and called Rav Amram a fool.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: Challenged Rabba's use of a money ruling for a ritual matter.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end their marriage.
The ceremony that releases a childless widow from having to marry her late husband's brother.
A girl married off as a minor could refuse the marriage before coming of age; a document recorded her refusal.
A question of what is permitted or forbidden, such as marriage, as opposed to a question of money.

13.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi came to the orchard of Mari bar Isak, and his sharecropper set dates and pomegranates before them. Ameimar and Rav Ashi ate; Mar Zutra did not. Mari bar Isak arrived and asked his sharecropper why he hadn't brought the Sages the better fruit. Ameimar and Rav Ashi asked Mar Zutra why he still would not eat. He answered in Rava's name that such words show an owner's consent only for teruma, a mitzva he is glad to see done; here the owner spoke out of embarrassment.
13.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that an owner who says 'you should have taken the better produce' consents to an agent's teruma; the Sages here argue over whether the same words prove consent for ordinary fruit.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: Ate the fruit the sharecropper served.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Would not eat the fruit, doubting the owner had agreed.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ate the fruit and questioned Mar Zutra.

people.name: Mari bar Isak
people.about: Owner of the orchard.

terms.meaning: A portion of the harvest given to a priest.
A tenant who farms someone else's land for a share of the crop.
A commandment, or a good deed done in fulfillment of one.

14.note: A silver goblet was stolen from the host of Mar Zutra Ḥasida. Mar Zutra saw a student wash his hands and dry them on someone else's cloak, and said this was the one who does not care about other people's property. He bound the student, and the student confessed.

people.name: Mar Zutra Ḥasida
people.about: A Sage whose host's goblet was stolen, and who found the thief.

terms.meaning: An epithet meaning "the pious."

15.note: A man found four dinars tied in a cloth that had been thrown into the Biran River. He came before Rav Yehuda, who told him to go and announce his find. The Gemara explains: things swept off by water usually belong to the finder, but this river has obstacles, so the owner does not give up hope; and though most people there are gentiles, Jews dammed the river and Jews dredge it, so the coins probably fell from a Jew who expects them back.
15.why: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that things lost to the sea, or where crowds gather, belong to the finder because the owner gives up hope; the Gemara asks whether Rav Yehuda's ruling limits that even where most people are gentiles.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who told the finder to announce the coins.

terms.meaning: A silver coin.
To announce publicly that one has found an item, so its owner can claim it.
The owner's giving up hope of getting a lost item back; once he does, the finder may keep it.

16.note: A kite snatched meat in the marketplace and dropped it among the palm trees of the house of bar Maryon. The man who found it asked Abaye, who told him to take it for himself. The Gemara explains that something carried off by a kite is like something swept away by the sea, which the owner gives up on, and that the meat was not forbidden as unwatched because the finder stood and saw it the whole time.
16.why: The Gemara is testing whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's rule, that a finder keeps items lost where the owner gives up hope, holds even where most people are Jews, as in a kosher meat market.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who let the finder keep the meat.

terms.meaning: A bird of prey.
Rav's rule that meat left unwatched is forbidden, since no one can be sure where it came from.

17.note: Rabbi Ḥanina found a slaughtered young goat between Tiberias and Tzippori, and the Sages permitted it to him. Rabbi Ami explained: they let him keep it as a found item, following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and let him eat it as properly slaughtered, following Rabbi Ḥananya son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who permits lost animals that their owner later finds slaughtered.
17.why: The Gemara is asking where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's rule applies; it goes on to infer from this case that the place had a Jewish majority, and Rava answers that only most of the slaughterers there were Jews.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Found the slaughtered goat.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Explained on what grounds the Sages permitted it.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥananya, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: Permits lost animals found slaughtered.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Forbids lost animals found slaughtered.

terms.meaning: Killed in the ritual way that makes meat kosher; meat from an animal not slaughtered properly is forbidden.
A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna.

18.note: Rabbi Ami found slaughtered fledglings between Tiberias and Tzippori. He asked Rabbi Asi (some say Rabbi Yoḥanan, some say the study hall) and was told to take them for himself. Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa found a skein of netting thread and asked Rabbi Yoḥanan (some say the study hall), and was told the same.
18.why: These continue a run of finds that the Sages let the finder keep, in line with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view that owners give up hope of things lost where crowds pass.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Found slaughtered fledglings on the road.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: One of those said to have told Rabbi Ami to keep them.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Asked about both finds, by some accounts.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: Found a skein of thread used for nets.

terms.meaning: A loose coil of thread or yarn.

19.note: Rav Pappa's father lost a donkey, and others found it. He came before Rabba bar Rav Huna, who told him to bring witnesses that he was not a swindler. He brought them, and Rabba bar Rav Huna asked: do you know that he is a swindler? They said yes. Rav Pappa's father cried out: I am a swindler? They said they had meant that he was not one. Rabba bar Rav Huna said that was reasonable, since a person does not bring witnesses against himself.
19.why: The Sages ruled that once swindlers multiplied, a claimant must bring witnesses that he is no swindler before taking back a lost item; this incident shows the rule in practice.

people.name: Rav Pappa's father
people.about: Lost a donkey and had to prove he was not a swindler.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: The judge who required witnesses and then accepted them.

terms.meaning: Someone known for false claims; the Sages would not return a lost item to him even if he described its marks.

20.note: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei was walking on the road when he met a man who had set down a load of wood and was resting. The man asked him to lift it onto him. Rabbi Yishmael asked what it was worth, paid him the half-dinar, and declared the wood ownerless. The man took the wood again, and Rabbi Yishmael again paid and declared it ownerless. When he saw the man wanted to take it once more, he said: I made it ownerless for everyone, but not for you.
20.why: Rava has just said a person must help load another's burden only where he would load his own; the Gemara goes on to ask how Rabbi Yishmael could exclude one man, and why he bothered, given that an elderly Sage was exempt.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage asked by a stranger to help lift his load of wood.

terms.meaning: Property declared free for anyone to take.
Half of a silver coin; the price the man named for his wood.
